member.name: T:Microsoft.VisualBasic.Engine.Particles.Boids.FlockGrid
member.summary: Dense uniform spatial grid built with counting sort.

remarks.para: The legacy implementation rebuilt the generic Grid(Of T()) spatial hash (a nested dictionary of dictionaries) every frame via LINQ GroupBy, and every neighbor lookup probed that dictionary-of-dictionaries nine times. At 80k boids that is ~1.4M dictionary probes plus hundreds of thousands of allocations per frame.

This grid is rebuilt every frame in O(N): one pass computes the rounded cell coordinate of every boid (the same ``CInt(x / cellSize)`` banker's rounding the legacy code used), one counting pass produces the CSR-style offsets, and one fill pass writes boid ids into grouped by cell. Boid ids inside a cell keep their original ascending order, so the neighbor enumeration order is identical to the legacy grid.

The grid is padded by one cell on each side of the per-frame bounding box. Because the wall bounce rule only applies a steering force (it never clamps positions), boids can drift outside the canvas; the padding preserves the legacy behavior where such out-of-bounds boids can still see each other as neighbors.

member.name: T:Microsoft.VisualBasic.Engine.Particles.Boids.FlockGrid3D
member.summary: Dense uniform spatial grid in three dimensions, built with counting sort.

remarks.para: This is the three dimensional counterpart of : one pass computes the rounded cell coordinate of every boid, one counting pass produces the CSR style offsets and one fill pass writes the boid ids into grouped by cell. Boid ids inside a cell keep their original ascending order, so the neighbor enumeration is deterministic.

The grid is padded by one cell on every side of the per frame bounding box, for the very same reason as in the two dimensional grid: the wall rule only applies a steering force and never clamps a position, so a boid can drift outside of the box and still has to see its neighbors.

Compared with the two dimensional version this grid adds two robustness guards that a three dimensional field makes necessary: a position whose cell coordinate would leave the valid range of is treated as a bad position, and the cell count is validated before the arrays are allocated - a sparse distribution over a huge volume would otherwise either overflow the integer index or exhaust the memory. A cell size that is too small for the current spread is silently enlarged, which degrades the neighbor search into a coarser grid instead of failing.

member.name: T:Microsoft.VisualBasic.Engine.Particles.FluidEngine3D
member.summary:
A 3D Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) fluid simulation engine.
This is the three dimensional counterpart of the 2D . The simulation pipeline of one (sub) step is:
1. apply the external forces (gravity + shake disturbance) and predict positions 2. rebuild the flat uniform grid () for the neighbour search 3. calculate the density and near density of each particle 4. calculate the pressure force (momentum conserving symmetric form) 5. calculate the viscosity force (density normalized, clamped) 6. integrate, then resolve the boundary / moving impeller constraints
The fluid is contained inside an which defaults to the axis aligned box volume [0,BoxSize.x] x [0,BoxSize.y] x [0,BoxSize.z] and gravity pulls the water along (by default the +Y face, i.e. the bottom of the legacy box container). Cylindrical vessels () and rotating impellers () can be plugged in for stirred tank scenarios.
member.remarks: Optimized revision: the particle state has been moved from an array of objects into Structure-of-Arrays buffers (), the spatial hash from a Dictionary(Of (Integer,Integer,Integer), ...) into a counting sorted flat grid, and every pass is now a race free gather (read only neighbourhood, write only into the own slot) so that the Parallel.For passes are deterministic and match the CUDA backend.

member.name: T:Microsoft.VisualBasic.Engine.Particles.FluidKernels
member.summary:
SPH smoothing kernels shared by the 2D solver and the 3D solver .
The five kernel *functions* are strictly identical in two and in three dimensions -- what differs is only the five normalization scaling factors, which is why this single type carries a switch instead of being duplicated into a 2D and a 3D flavour.
IMPORTANT: the normalization constant is WHERE THE DIMENSION ACTUALLY LIVES. It is not possible to emulate a 2D simulation with the 3D code by simply pinning the z coordinate to zero: the kernels are normalized against ∫W dV = 1, and the integration measure is 2πr·dr in 2D but 4πr²·dr in 3D. The resulting constants do not merely differ by a factor, they differ by a whole power of h (i.e. by their physical dimension: 1/area vs 1/volume). Feeding 3D constants into a 2D solver makes the density estimate -- and therefore every pressure term -- systematically wrong.
The exact constants, obtained from ∫ (h-r)^n · 2πr dr (2D) and ∫ (h-r)^n · 4πr² dr (3D) over r ∈ [0,h]:
+ Poly6 (h²-r²)³ : 2D ∫ = πh⁸/4 → 4 / (PI * h^8) 3D ∫ = 64πh⁹/315 → 315 / (64 * PI * h^9) + SpikyPow3 (h-r)³ : 2D ∫ = πh⁵/10 → 10 / (PI * h^5) 3D ∫ = πh⁶/15 → 15 / (PI * h^6) + SpikyPow2 (h-r)² : 2D ∫ = πh⁴/6 → 6 / (PI * h^4) 3D ∫ = 2πh⁵/15 → 15 / (2 * PI * h^5) + d/dr SpikyPow3 -3(h-r)² : 2D → 30 / (PI * h^5) 3D → 45 / (PI * h^6) + d/dr SpikyPow2 -2(h-r) : 2D → 12 / (PI * h^4) 3D → 15 / (PI * h^5)
NOTE: the SpikyPow2 pair of the 3D solver was previously normalized with the 2D-derived constants (15/(PI*h^5) and 30/(PI*h^5)), which are exactly 2x too large in three dimensions. That factor of two made the pressure term of inconsistent with the near-pressure term and is one of the reasons why the original 3D solver looked unstable.
The scaling factors depend only on the smoothing radius (and the dimension), so they are precomputed once in the constructor.
